title: Twelve Days of Gifts: The Leaders Dedicate the Altar
summary: When the tabernacle is set up, the twelve tribal leaders give six covered carts and twelve oxen, which Moses distributes to the Levite clans that carry the heavy parts of the Tent. Then, one leader per day for twelve days, each tribe presents an identical set of gifts for the dedication of the altar: silver and gold vessels, grain, incense, and animals for sacrifice. The chapter totals the gifts and ends with Moses hearing God's voice from above the ark.
story: Chapter 7 steps back in time. It opens “On the day Moses finished setting up the tabernacle”, which Exodus 40:17 dates to the first day of the first month of the second year, a month before the census of Numbers 1:1. The book places it here because it completes what chapters 1 to 6 began. The tribes have been counted and arranged, the Levites have been given their loads, and now the tribes themselves contribute: the means for moving the tabernacle and the gifts for its altar. The twelve leaders named in chapters 1 and 2 appear once more, in the same order in which they camp and march. The chapter's final verse then shows the purpose of it all. Moses enters the Tent, and God speaks.
historical:
The setting is Sinai at the completion of the tabernacle, and the chapter reads like an archival record, the kind of exact inventory that temples across the ancient Near East kept of gifts received. It lists the weight of every vessel and the number of every animal, then totals them. Each silver platter weighed 130 shekels, perhaps about three pounds, and each bowl 70 shekels, measured by the sanctuary shekel, the standard weight associated with the sanctuary.

Later dedications in Israel's history follow the same pattern on a larger scale. When Solomon dedicated the temple, the text records 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep as peace offerings (1 Kings 8:63). The Hebrew word for dedication here, chanukkah, later gave its name to the Jewish festival that remembers the rededication of the Jerusalem temple in 164 BC, after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV had desecrated it.
cultural:
The carts and oxen are practical gifts. Moses gives the Gershonites, who carried the fabrics, two carts and four oxen, and the Merarites, who carried the heavy frames, posts, and bases, four carts and eight oxen. The Kohathites receive none, because the holy furnishings had to be carried on their shoulders (verse 9). Generations later, when David moved the ark on a new cart, the result was the death of Uzzah (2 Samuel 6:3-7), and David came to see that the ark should have been carried as this law prescribed (1 Chronicles 15:13-15).

The dedication gifts cover every kind of sacrifice in Israel's worship. The burnt offering, wholly consumed on the altar, expressed complete dedication to God. The sin offering dealt with impurity and wrongdoing. The peace offerings, by far the largest part, were shared meals in which most of the meat was eaten by the worshipers before God. Grain mixed with oil and incense accompanied them. To give all of these was to open every avenue of Israel's worship at once. Oxen and rams were valuable property, and the tribes gave them in large numbers: 252 animals in all.
literary: Numbers 7 has 89 verses, making it the longest chapter in the Torah and, after Psalm 119, the longest in the English Bible. Most of its length comes from a single paragraph of six verses repeated twelve times with only the day, the name, and the tribe changed. A modern editor would have written one paragraph and added that each leader gave the same. The Bible does not, and the repetition is the point. Every tribe's gift is recorded in full, no tribe's offering is summarized as a copy of another's, and none outdoes the others. Jewish interpreters have long seen this as honoring each leader individually. The chapter moves from the carts (verses 1-9), through the twelve days (verses 10-83), to the totals (verses 84-88), and then to a single verse about God's voice. After twelve days of human giving, the climax is God speaking.

outline.t: The leaders bring carts and oxen
The carts given to the Gershonites and Merarites
One leader each day for the altar's dedication
The totals of the dedication gifts
God speaks to Moses from above the mercy seat

doctrines.note: Every tribe gives, every gift is recorded, and no tribe is ranked above another in its giving. Worship is the whole people's work, and each part of the people is honored in its own name.

Each day's gift includes a sin offering along with the burnt and peace offerings. Even at the joyful dedication of the altar, Israel approaches God on the basis of atonement, the covering of sin and impurity that he himself provided.

The chapter ends with Moses hearing “the voice speaking to him from between the two cherubim above the mercy seat” (verse 89), fulfilling God's promise in Exodus 25:22 to meet and speak there. The tabernacle exists so that God can speak with his people.

words.note: Chanukkah, dedication. The word marks the formal opening of something for its purpose, and it is used of the altar here and of the temple and Jerusalem's walls later (Nehemiah 12:27). It gave its name to the Jewish festival of Hanukkah, the Feast of Dedication mentioned in John 10:22.

Qorban, offering, from the verb qarav, to draw near. An offering is literally something brought near to God, and each leader in this chapter “drew near” with his gift. The word appears in the Gospels as Corban, a gift devoted to God, when Jesus criticizes those who used such vows to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:11).

Kapporet, the mercy seat or atonement cover, the gold lid of the ark with a cherub at each end. It is related to the verb kipper, to atone, and it was the place where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. In verse 89 it is the place from which God speaks. The Greek translation called it hilasterion, the word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25.

christ: John records that Jesus was in the temple at the Feast of Dedication (John 10:22-23), the festival whose name comes from this chapter's word for the altar's dedication. There, speaking of himself as “the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” (John 10:36), he presented himself as the one truly set apart for God. The chapter's many repeated sacrifices also belong to the picture Hebrews draws of a priesthood that must “offer again and again the same sacrifices” (Hebrews 10:11), set against Christ, who “offered for all time one sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12). Most striking is verse 89. The place from which God spoke was the mercy seat, and Paul uses the Greek word for that place when he says God “presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood” (Romans 3:25). The place where God met his people and spoke is, in the New Testament's reading, fulfilled in the person of Christ, through whom “in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son” (Hebrews 1:2).

hard.q: Why does the Bible repeat the same list of gifts twelve times instead of summarizing it?
hard.a: Modern readers often find this chapter the hardest in the Bible to read, and the question is fair. Several answers work together. The chapter preserves the style of an ancient archival record, where each donor's gift was entered separately and in full. Its repetition is also theological. By giving each tribe the same space and the same words, the text shows that no tribe's gift is worth less and none is a mere copy; each leader drew near to God in his own name on his own day. Some Jewish interpreters went further, finding a distinct meaning in each identical offering tied to that tribe's history, though that is interpretation rather than the text's own claim. Finally, the repetition slows the reader down to the pace of the event itself, twelve days of worship, before the single short verse in which God speaks. The length is not an accident; it is part of what the chapter says.

questions: Every tribe brought the same gift, and every gift was recorded in full. What does that suggest about how God regards the offerings of people who give the same as everyone else?
The chapter spends 88 verses on human giving and one on God speaking. What is the relationship between worship and hearing God?
The Kohathites were given no carts because some things had to be carried by hand. What in your life of faith cannot be made easier by tools or shortcuts?
